name: Pauncy Green
lede: Pauncy Green is a muted, mid-toned olive green, a Maerz and Paul dictionary name from 1930 that the dictionary traces, under related names, back to the year 1600.

sections.title: An old green under new names
sections.body:
The Maerz and Paul dictionary of 1930 records "Pauncy Green" itself undated on plate 22 D 8, but the same chart spot carries older names: Flower de Luce Green from 1600, Pancy Green from 1654 and Iris Green from about 1864 [1]. That spread of names and dates, all clustered on one plate position, shows how often fabric and paint trades renamed the same green over three centuries [1].

The nearest named colors on file are [[fern-green]], [[hay-s-green]], [[dark-sage]] and [[velvet-green]], at 3.1, 4.1, 4.5 and 4.9 ΔE [1]. Who coined "pauncy" itself, or what it meant, is undocumented in the books we hold [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, as photographed, this olive green appears in 144, about 0.61 percent, more common than 54 percent of our named colors [2]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 22 of 1,674 paintings, at 3.9 times the expected rate, and it is most over-represented in paintings from France, at 2.8 times the expected rate [2]. Inside a painting it most often plays an accent rather than a light or a shadow [2].

[[painter:camille-pissarro|Camille Pissarro]] is its most devoted painter, present in 4 of his 50 works here, 5.4 times his museums' baseline [2]. The earliest match is a 1357 painting, about two and a half centuries before the earliest name on its chart spot, so that early hit is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof of the dye, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2].

openers: One chart spot carries four different green names spanning over 250 years: Flower de Luce Green, Pancy Green, Iris Green and Pauncy Green.
